_comment: Evaluation corpus for tool search. Tools mirror the shape of real MCP
servers (names and one-line descriptions of the kind those servers ship).
METHODOLOGY, and the thing that makes this worth anything: queries are
written in the vocabulary a USER or AGENT would use, NOT by copying words
out of the tool they are supposed to find. A query built from the target's
own description measures nothing except that substring matching works.
Each query is tagged:
lexical  - shares real vocabulary with the target; a good lexical
scorer should find it, and failure here is a genuine bug.
semantic - needs synonym or world knowledge ('bug report' -> issue,
'save this' -> memory_store). Largely out of reach for any
lexical scorer; tracked separately so it is never mistaken
for lexical headroom, and so we can see what embeddings
would actually buy.
`expect` lists every answer a reasonable person would accept.
heldout  - written AFTER the synonym table and never consulted while
building it. The generalisation check, and the one to
believe: the semantic group scores its own training set.
HELD-OUT ROUND 2 (2026-07-24), written to FALSIFY a candidate change.
The open miss was 'what do you know about this project' -> memory_recall,
which returned memory_forget_topic because only the word 'about' matched
anything at all. Mapping know -> recall would clear it — but that query is
in the semantic (training) group, and the held-out group contained no query
using 'know', so a flat held-out score would have proved nothing either way.
So twelve queries were added BEFORE measuring, three of which use 'know'
while wanting something other than memory ('know which tables exist',
'let me know what time it is', 'know who is in this channel'). If a
know -> recall mapping is too broad, those are what say so.
Honest caveat: the author knew the synonym table, so these are not blind.
Their power comes from being adversarial, not from ignorance — a query
written to break your idea is worth more than one written to confirm it.
